12. VII 1941
Dear Hanna, and Manfred,
We have not heard from you this week but I suppose
a letter is on its way. Now we are every day expecting
a cable telling us that Manfred passed his exam, and we look
forward to knowing you in Bath for a long and well-deserved
rest. It really looks now as if that parcel Eva and I sent
together in April, has been lost. I sent another one to London
about 2 or 3 weeks ago, and a small one to mother and Ursula
whose birthday must have been one of these days. They come
all from Altman's and you may have to pay a small amount
of duty. - We have had Eva with us last Saturday until
Tuesday, and I was with her in London on Monday to see the
dentist. I shall take her once more Thursday next, and then
she will be finished. There was not much to be done. Eva
looks splendid, very brown and strong. She liked being with
us and read the whole book "The Microbe-Hunters" by Kruif
while she was here. If there are no special holiday events
in Amity Hall we will take her again for a few days
before or after we go to New York. - Stefan is working very hard
partly because he wanted to work, partly because he is depressed
by the facts of war in their humanity-destroying consequences,
partly because there is nothing else to be done here. It is nice,
green and quiet out here, but that is about all. If you
have no car there is nothing to be seen and nothing to be
done. This and many other, more important reasons may
decide us in the not too far future to return to Brazil.
For how long we can not say yet. Should we not return to the
States within a few months and the war go on and on, we might
want to take Eva to stay with us there. I need not say how much
I would like to have her with me, but I am afraid she might
find it much harder to adapt herself to Brazil. It would mean
passing from one extreme to the other, from the most liberal
education methods to old-fashioned ones, not to speak of the
new language she would have to learn. I enquired about
schools before I left Rio; there is one American school which

teaches in English and the American curriculum. But I am not
sure that it still exists now. I heard that all foreign
language newspapers had been suppressed, and they may have
closed that school, too. All the other schools teach Portuguese
only although a few years ago they had (in)
some of them taught partly Portuguese, partly English and
French. - I am afraid I upset you much too soon with
discussions of far-away possibilities. For the moment we are
not even quite sure that we will go, but if we go, we
might decide rather suddenly, and I want you to feel that
we think of Eva while making our plans, although the plans
unfortunately are influenced by quite other reasons.
Should she have to stay on you may be sure that with
Mrs. Sch. she is in very best care and that all the others
who would also look after her, my sister-in-law Rose,
Elizabeth, would have nothing more to do than to take
her out now and then and spoil her a little. Mrs. Sch.
thinks of giving up their present place and of taking a
bigger and much better equipped house also in Croton.
Eva will without doubt tell you all about it in her
letters. As to changing her school Miss Baker and others
assured me that there was no need for it at present.
The situation is to a certain degree similar to that in
England, Public Schools being good yet not considered
the same as Private Schools from a certain snobbishness.
But at Eva's age there is no difference yet and no need
for change.
Love and kisses
Lotte.
Dear Hanna & Manfred, we have nothing decided yet but there are
offers for new lectures, my book will there will be publisher and other
reasons; I think also about Lotte who does not like the climate here
with its continual sudden changes. All is now difficult to decide and
the future darkened by the prospect of a long and still more cruel war
Lotte is right in saying that I am extremely depressed, this nomadic
life is difficult to bear in my age; I want so sincerely a little rest
and more concentration. For Eva I have no fear, she feels there perfectly

result.confidence_notes: Der Text ist sehr gut lesbar, trotz der handschriftlichen Kursivschrift. Die Archivierungshilfen auf dem letzten Scan verdecken Teile des Textes, die jedoch durch den Scan ohne Hilfsmittel (Seite 3) vollständig rekonstruierbar sind.
